# Calendar, density and significance checks {#numerical-validation}

A01, D01 and S03 tested the unmodified skyscapeR **2.0.9005** source archive, SHA-256 `0446c0a57afe16274e7ef033113ac8d9f251b4f812b1a2d2ea22eac145bb3bbe`. [Download the exact tested package](archives/skyscapeR_2.0.9005.tar.gz). D01 and S03 were subsequently rerun on [build 2.0.9006](archives/skyscapeR_2.0.9006.tar.gz), SHA-256 `0a97b65385bb253b75b287f160b6e79da63a0ddae29b6be31c5ad6902c6cd6d2`. Each study uses a numerical reference independent of the implementation under test. Each archive contains the scripts, expected and observed quantities and reproduction instructions. The previous chapters identify the builds used for their own examples.

## A01 · Calendar, clock and angular conventions {#a01-calendar-checks}

**Question.** Can a civil date or historical era label be placed on the correct UT Julian date and converted back with the intended clock, calendar and sign?

**Outcome.** All 499 assertions passed. The test compared 240 absolute Julian dates and independently checked 240 returned civil strings. The maximum difference in the Julian-date comparisons was 0.000021 seconds, below the 0.0001-second tolerance. The remaining 19 assertions covered era parsing and formatting, angular signs, clock changes, invalid inputs, midnight rounding and session settings.

We computed the Julian day number by integer Gregorian or Julian calendar arithmetic, with the day starting at noon, then applied the stated clock offset. Reference anchors included J2000 noon (JD 2451545.0), the Unix epoch at midnight (JD 2440587.5) and the Julian epoch at noon (JD 0). Ten dates from astronomical year −4712 to CE 2024, four times of day, both proleptic calendars and three fixed offsets (−03:30, UTC and +05:45) formed the crossed grid. The inverse checks supplied reference JDs directly to the package. The [JPL J2000 definition](https://naif.jpl.nasa.gov/pub/naif/toolkit_docs/C/cspice/j2000_c.html) supplies an external anchor.

The London checks included the missing and repeated 01:30 local times on the 2024 clock-change dates; both produced errors, as documented. Year zero, Julian leap-year behaviour, a negative sub-degree angle, a date rounded across midnight, argument overrides and restoration of session timezone were also exercised. These checks cover civil-time conversion; they provide no constraint on prehistoric ΔT or the accuracy of every historical timezone database entry.

[Download A01 code, fixtures and all 499 results](archives/A01-verification.zip). [Calendar and angle methods](astronomical-conventions.qmd) · [Validation programme](study-register.qmd#validation-programme).

## D01 · Measurement densities, sums and highest-density regions {#d01-density-checks}

**Question.** Do sampled measurement densities retain the expected shape, mass and circular support, and do summaries and subsets retain the intended observation?

**Extension · 2.0.9011.** Checks of the [six measurement families](orientation-densities.qmd#measurement-families) compare sampled ordinates with analytic values, integrate the four new doorway examples, check an asymmetric triangle across north, and compare a broad wrapped convolution with a periodic reference. A deterministic model at the observed bearings or declinations reproduces the empirical SPD for each new family after subsetting and reordering. All 173 original D01 assertions and 13 supplemental assertions also passed on this build. [Download the family checks and the repeated D01 results](archives/D01-9011-density-families.zip).

**Earlier outcome · 2.0.9006.** All 173 original assertions passed, including the 18 previous discrepancies. Thirteen further checks verified broad wrapped Gaussians, the closing segment of interpolated azimuth sums and equivalent input bearings. A 0.005° grid now retains 359.995° at its own bearing. Gaussian contributions and all copies of a uniform support interval are combined at each bearing before applying the density cutoff. Declination subsets now carry centres in the selected order, including repeated and empty selections. [Download the corrected D01 run](archives/D01-9006-rerun.zip).

**Previous run · 2.0.9005.** Of 173 assertions, 155 passed and 18 showed differences. Of 144 ordinary-width sampled-density comparisons, 132 agreed. All 12 differences occurred at the north seam on the 0.005° grid. The two additional broad-width cases and four declination-centre metadata checks also differed. The archive retains all residuals, including failures.

For each coordinate we evaluated Gaussian and uniform densities directly from their analytic definitions. Azimuth distances were taken around the circle, while declination was confined to [−90°, 90°]. The matrix comprised four azimuth centres and five declination centres, uncertainty 2°, four grid spacings and two density cutoffs. We compared every retained value, total grid mass and the first two moments about the centre. An independent numerical integral checked the retained Gaussian mass at three spacings. The summed and unit-area normalised SPDs agreed in the tested cases. Known highest-density regions, including disconnected supports and ties at threshold, returned the expected endpoints and reached the requested mass. For equal-height modes, retaining the full tied set can exceed the target mass. These are discrete-grid checks of the PDFs in the framework of @silva2020.

| Finding on build 2.0.9005 | Consequence |
|---|---|
| On the 0.005° azimuth grid, the implementation folds samples above 359.99° across north. Twelve narrow-density cases centred at 359°, 0° or 1° differed from the periodic reference. | Density can be displaced across the seam. For the 0° Gaussian, the maximum pointwise discrepancy was 0.19947 per degree even though the integrated mass was nearly unchanged. |
| A 100° uniform half-width and a Gaussian standard deviation of 100° both exceeded the effective 90° margin used for folding. | The resulting curves omit part of the periodic density. A grid-spacing change alone cannot recover those tails. |
| Selecting the second declination PDF, reversing the order, repeating a selection or selecting no rows retained the original declination-centre vector. | The selected curves and names followed the requested order. Reading `metadata$dec` as the centres of the selected curves can misidentify an observation. |

[Download D01 code, residuals and moments](archives/D01-verification.zip). [Measurement density methods](orientation-densities.qmd) · [Validation programme](study-register.qmd#validation-programme).

## S03 · Monte Carlo ranks, local clusters and reported probabilities {#s03-scoring-checks}

**Question.** Given the same observed and simulated curves, do the two significance tests report the expected global rank, local clusters and adjusted probabilities?

**Current outcome · 2.0.9006.** The independent scorer agreed on global ranks, local endpoints and adjusted probabilities in all 19 comparisons. These include the two original public simulation matrices replayed unchanged. All 88 binomial, print, symbol and plot assertions passed. The count fell from 92 because the two example fits now each report one cluster across north. Twelve additional checks confirmed invariance of the ranks to rotation of the angular origin and agreement between memory and disk scoring. [Download the corrected S03 run](archives/S03-9006-rerun.zip).

On the original `randomTest()` curves, the corrected global probability is **0.4375** and the **349.5°–10°** excess has adjusted **p = 0.1875**. On the original `modelTest()` curves the corrected excess spans **346°–15°**, with global and adjusted local **p = 0.0625**. A start bearing greater than the end bearing denotes a single interval running clockwise through north. The uniform-bearing null samples north once; the global score counts each direction once, and the observed curve and every simulated curve undergo the same circular cluster search. The repeated endpoint may still appear in the display. Declination ranges remain linear. Stored fits from previous builds retain their original probabilities; refit the original input data to obtain current inference.

**Previous run · 2.0.9005.** Independent enumeration reproduced every global probability, local interval and adjusted local probability in 17 linear-grid cases. These included fixed fixtures and seeded calls through both public functions. All 92 separate assertions on binomial probabilities, symbol thresholds, printed results and plotted cluster marks passed. A circular reference exposed a seam effect on the local results and, in one seeded fit, on the global p-value.

The Python reference pooled the observed and simulated values at each coordinate, computed sample standard deviations and interpolated quantiles, and ranked the sum of standardised excursions. One-tail tests used upper excursions and two-tail tests also included lower excursions. For each simulated curve the reference selected its own largest qualifying cluster before ranking the observed local score. The discrete reference included ties, all-identical curves, an isolated excursion, clusters on both sides, and spans at and just below 0.5°. For public calls, the R harness recorded the actual simulation matrix passed to inference; Python then scored it independently. This isolates the scoring stage from the null-generation and power studies scheduled under S01 and S02.

**What changed since the published algorithms?** Silva (2020) used simulation-only bounds and scored simulations over the observed local interval. Silva & Lomsdalen (2025) extended testing to shared and site-specific null models. The present functions pool the observation with simulations, include tied exceedances, use the positive rank floor and search for the largest cluster in every simulation [@silva2020; @silvaloms2025]. On a fixed set of 16 curves, a reconstruction of the archived 2020 scoring equations gave global p = 0 and local p = 0 for the excess over 2–9°. Build 2.0.9005 gave 0.125 for both with the same curves. In a separate eight-simulation example with zero exceedances, the positive floor was 1/9. This comparison concerns scoring on controlled inputs. The original archaeological datasets were not reanalysed. [Historical implementation and methodological comparison](significance.qmd#sig-history).

**North seam on 2.0.9005.** The earlier build searches the azimuth grid as a line, splitting a north-crossing excess into separate intervals. A circular diagnostic joined the first and last runs and counted the duplicated 0°/360° direction once. In the seeded 15-simulation `randomTest()` example, the package gave global p = 0.375 and separate intervals 349.5–360° (adjusted p = 0.750) and 0–10° (p = 0.9375). The circular comparison gave global p = 0.4375 and one 349.5–10° interval (p = 0.1875). The small number of simulations makes the arithmetic transparent. These values illustrate sensitivity to the seam and supply no estimate of false-positive frequency. Declination has physical endpoints and uses the linear comparison.

## A04 · Crossing times, bearings and event order {#a04-stellar-crossings}

At 50° N, 0° longitude and sea level, we disabled refraction and compared the crossing solver with the spherical altitude equation. For a track of declination zero, the expected azimuths on a level skyline are 90° and 270°. We then raised the entire skyline to 5°, and finally raised only the eastern sector to 5° across the rising point. The table gives the returned azimuths in degrees clockwise from north.

| Skyline | Zero-declination rise | Zero-declination set | Mintaka rise | Mintaka set |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Level at 0° | 90.00000 | 270.00000 | 89.53811 | 270.46193 |
| Level at 5° | 95.98482 | 264.01518 | 95.51882 | 264.48122 |
| Eastern ridge only | 95.98482 | 270.00000 | 95.51882 | 270.46193 |

The prescribed track exercised the internal crossing solver. The named-star cases exercised [`riseset()`](help/riseset.html) on 1 January 2000 UTC. Mintaka’s reference used its noon declination from the same ephemeris and an independent spherical calculation. Polaris returned missing rise and set records on the eastern-ridge profile. All 14 event checks passed on 2.0.9006. The maximum absolute azimuth discrepancy was below 0.000001° for the prescribed track and below 0.000022° for Mintaka, against a tolerance of 0.001°. The extended study added 137 assertions, all of which passed.

At latitudes 50° N and 35° S, we compared event counts, direction, order, times and bearings with a one-second scan and independently bisected roots on flat, uniformly raised, notched, ridge and step-like skylines. All 28 reference crossings were recovered with no extras. The maximum timing discrepancy was 0.00038 s against a tolerance of 0.02 s. Flat and raised times also agreed with the closed-form hour-angle solution. A constructed touch without a sign change produced no event; a two-second emergence produced both roots.

On 2 January 2000, a ridge at 50° N, 100° E produced rise, set and re-emergence for Mintaka. The public function selected the first rise and first set independently with refraction both on and off. Independent five-second ephemeris scans located the same events within the 1.1 s allowance for whole-second output. Polaris returned no events at either 50° N (always above) or 50° S (always below). A lunar rise after the next local midnight returned the following date in UTC−02:30.

At 35.90083° N, 14.34° E, we compared geometric centre crossings for the Sun and Moon with [JPL Horizons](https://ssd.jpl.nasa.gov/horizons/). The reference interpolates airless topocentric direction vectors and solves for clearance above the skyline. We tested both scalar and profile representations of a flat skyline and an asymmetric profile. The largest discrepancies were 0.842 s and 0.00410°, within the 3 s and 0.015° comparison tolerances. Doubling the reference sampling interval from 10 to 20 minutes moved the reference times by less than 0.001 s. The tolerances allow for whole-second timestamps and differing ephemeris conventions. These are tests of centre crossings. First limb contact and naked-eye visibility require different definitions.

[Download the reproduction scripts, input checksums and results for A04 and D02](archives/skyscapeR-9006-A04-D02-validation.zip).

## D02 · Bearing uncertainty on flat and irregular skylines {#d02-bearing-propagation}

We tested [`coordtrans()`](help/coordtrans.html) at 50° N with a constant 2° skyline and refraction disabled. Bearings had a Gaussian standard deviation of 2° about centres of 90°, 359° and 0°. Independent Gaussian altitude errors had a standard deviation of 0.5°. For each centre, we transformed one million paired draws through the spherical altitude equation and compared the median and both endpoints of the equal-tailed 95% interval with the package density. We used the same seeded draws at each centre.

At calculation and azimuth integration spacings of 0.1° and 0.05°, all 18 quantile comparisons fell within the specified 0.02° tolerance. The largest absolute discrepancy was 0.00505°, at the upper endpoint for a bearing centred on north on the coarser grid. All six returned densities integrated to one within 0.000001. The discrepancy includes Monte Carlo sampling variation. The extended study varied each numerical spacing separately. Ten configurations returned densities on five grids, and an eleventh tested the documented zero-width limit. The references were (1) direct spherical propagation of 524,288 scrambled Sobol draws and (2) independent quadrature over 8,192 bearing strata using the package’s endpoint-Gaussian implementation of the conditional-density method [@silva2020]. The refracted case shared the Swiss altitude correction to isolate propagation. The archive reports mass error, maximum CDF distance, quantiles, prominent modes and 80% highest-density regions.

| Configuration | Largest fine-grid quantile difference from direct propagation |
|:---|---:|
| Eastern slope rising / falling clockwise | 0.00152° / 0.00241° |
| Sloping skyline crossing north | 0.00089° |
| Asymmetric ridge with multiple modes | 0.00082° |
| Archived Kunċizzjoni terrain model | 0.00131° |
| Surveyed Canrooska skyline | 0.00023° |
| Refracted slope / doubled altitude uncertainty | 0.00754° / 0.00568° |
| Observer at geographic north pole | 0.00057° |
| Sightline near celestial pole | 0.17149° |

The Canrooska input linearly interpolates [surveyed bearings and altitudes](https://mega-what.com/sites/Canrooska/sitedata.htm) at the stone row. The Kunċizzjoni input uses Tore Lomsdalen’s archived Horizon terrain model. Across nine configurations away from the celestial-pole limit, all three quantiles on all five grids agreed with direct propagation within 0.008°. The maximum CDF distance was 0.00411. For the summed-density check, transforming a normalised sum of two bearing PDFs gave area 0.99999947. The integrated absolute difference from summing the two individually transformed PDFs was 0.00159 after normalisation.

**Grid sensitivity.** The ridge had three prominent modes near −0.77°, 3.87° and 9.89°. On the default grid, the 80% highest-density region split the middle band and returned four intervals. Reducing the calculation and azimuth integration steps to 0.05° and the output step to 0.005° recovered the three reference intervals. For this ridge, refining only the integration spacing reduced the largest quantile discrepancy from 0.00645° to 0.00245°. Refining only the calculation spacing reduced it to 0.00485°; refining only the output spacing gave 0.00642°.

**Celestial-pole limit.** At latitude 50° N with a 47° northern skyline, the fine-grid result differed from direct propagation by up to 0.1715° in quantiles and 0.0589 in cumulative probability. Agreement with independent integration of the conditional Gaussian was within 0.00070° in quantiles. The discrepancy is therefore primarily in that approximation. At a 50° northern skyline, the transformed endpoints coincide for the central bearing. The function raised its documented zero-width error on every grid even though direct propagation had a central 95% interval of 87.071°–89.819°. These cases distinguish the celestial-pole geometry from a geographic-pole observer, for which a density was recovered.

[Download the reproduction scripts, input checksums and results for A04 and D02](archives/skyscapeR-9006-A04-D02-validation.zip).

## S01 · Calibration of the uniform-orientation test {#s01-uniform-orientation}

How frequently does [`randomTest()`](help/randomTest.html) reject when orientations have been independently drawn from its stated uniform-bearing model? How frequently does it detect a cluster of known strength and width? We fixed the survey geometry, measurement widths, sample size and bearing support before drawing each dataset.

**Implementation check.** In 2.0.9006 the simulated PDFs used the constructor’s default spacing and cutoff. The shared-horizon simulation also summed the bearings at the default SPD spacing, whereas the observed sum used the requested spacing. With identical centres of 30° and 120°, widths of 22° and 32°, a 30° source grid, a 0.0001 source cutoff and a 2° test spacing, maximum absolute observed–simulated density differences were 0.00203 for azimuth, 0.02020 for the shared skyline and 0.17537 for site-paired declinations. On 2.0.9007 all three differences were zero. The correction can affect probabilities calculated with non-default source settings and the shared-horizon route whenever its selected SPD spacing differed from the simulation default. Refit affected analyses from their original inputs. The 2.0.9007 socket worker setup also resolves the parent library path on each worker. In a two-library installation, the corrected serial and two-worker results agreed exactly on all three routes.

**Design.** We ran 2,000 independent outer datasets in each of 13 null settings and four cluster alternatives. Every outer dataset had fresh Monte Carlo reference draws. Normal and uniform measurement families, sample sizes of 2 to 24, one and two tails, different grid widths and 9, 19, 39 or 99 simulations were represented. For each outer fit we recorded the global probability and the smallest maximum-cluster-adjusted probability across the reported intervals, assigning one when there was no interval. The preselected thresholds were 1%, 5% and 10%. Finite ranks have spacing $1/(B+1)$, with inclusive ranking for ties.

To make repeated calculations feasible we reused deterministic package-generated densities for each permitted bearing, width and site. For the shared route we tabulated the entire transform for every ordered input pair. A separate implementation scored the pooled observed and simulated curves. In 16 public-interface replays, all reconstructed curves agreed within $8\times10^{-15}$ in density and all global and minimum local probabilities agreed exactly. The shared-route design uses two observations and six or twelve possible directions. Its calibration applies to those designs.

**Null results.** Entries give the rejection percentage at the nominal 5% level, with pointwise 95% Wilson intervals over datasets. A local rejection means at least one adjusted interval crossed the threshold.

| Null setting | Global rejection | Any local rejection |
|:---|---:|---:|
| Azimuth, 12 bearings on a 6° grid | 4.50% (3.68–5.50) | 4.25% (3.45–5.23) |
| Azimuth, 12 bearings on a 0.01° grid | 5.35% (4.45–6.42) | 4.90% (4.04–5.94) |
| Two bearings, shared level skyline | 4.95% (4.08–5.99) | 4.75% (3.90–5.77) |
| Two bearings, shared rough skyline | 5.50% (4.58–6.59) | 5.70% (4.77–6.80) |
| Two bearings, shared rough skyline, 12 directions | 5.15% (4.26–6.21) | 5.10% (4.22–6.15) |
| 12 bearings paired with two different skylines | 4.25% (3.45–5.23) | 4.80% (3.95–5.83) |

Across all null settings in which a 5% rejection was attainable, global rates ranged from 4.25% to 5.85% and any-local rates from 4.25% to 5.85%. With nine simulations the smallest possible probability was 0.10, so no dataset could reject at 0.05. Results at 0.01 and 0.10, counts, confidence intervals, and every individual rank are in the reproduction archive.

**Power.** With twelve measurements and 39 simulations, injecting three bearings from a 24° standard-deviation cluster centred at north gave 9.30% global rejection. Injecting six at that width gave 30.35%. Narrowing the six-bearing cluster to 6° raised global rejection to 92.40% and any-local rejection to 93.70%. With site-paired transformations the same narrow injection gave 63.20% global rejection and 69.75% any-local rejection. These estimates describe the specified support, widths, horizons and alternatives. Each null result assumes independent orientations with the stated measurement model.

[Download the S01 reproduction scripts and all results](archives/S01-reproduction.zip). [Installable source tested in S01](archives/skyscapeR_2.0.9007.tar.gz), SHA-256 `5bfe20d6a5a440da8b732700d19eb2e7741032f1923622bfc0abdf999b366767`.

## S02 · Specified and site-specific null models {#s02-specified-models}

Can [`modelTest()`](help/modelTest.html) recover the expected false-positive rate when the proposed model gives different weights to candidate directions at different sites? The study used five unequally spaced candidate directions, weights interpreted as probability masses, eight observations and 39 fresh reference draws per fit. We tested azimuth densities, directly constructed declination densities and asymmetric templates shifted to candidate means.

**Same-input comparison.** In 2.0.9007, simulated azimuth and declination PDFs used constructor defaults even when the input PDF had been constructed on a different grid or with a different cutoff. With a 0.5° source grid and 0.002 cutoff the largest observed–simulated density discrepancy was 0.0015831 in both fixtures. The same draws on 2.0.9008 gave zero discrepancy. Public fits agreed with independent assembly of their observed and simulated curves and with independently scored global and local ranks. An independent first-moment calculation also checked asymmetric template shifting, explicit replacement uncertainties and the pole-boundary error. Two actual horizon-transformed PDFs agreed with independent shifts to within floating-point precision.

**Calibration.** Twelve conditions each used 2,000 independent outer datasets. The six matched null conditions give the following rejection rates at the 5% threshold; parentheses contain pointwise 95% Wilson intervals. Local rejection means that at least one adjusted cluster probability crossed the threshold.

| Coordinate or template | Input model | Global rejection | Any local rejection |
|:---|:---|---:|---:|
| Azimuth | Common weights | 5.00% (4.13–6.04) | 5.05% (4.17–6.10) |
| Azimuth | Site-specific weights | 4.55% (3.72–5.55) | 4.50% (3.68–5.50) |
| Declination | Common weights | 5.50% (4.58–6.59) | 5.20% (4.31–6.26) |
| Declination | Site-specific weights | 4.35% (3.54–5.33) | 4.05% (3.27–5.01) |
| Shifted asymmetric template | Common weights | 5.35% (4.45–6.42) | 5.25% (4.36–6.32) |
| Shifted asymmetric template | Site-specific weights | 5.35% (4.45–6.42) | 5.50% (4.58–6.59) |

Concentrating four of eight observations on the fourth candidate increased global rejection to 48.0–57.8% across the three routes. Pairing the random quantiles of two observations while retaining the site's marginal model increased global rejection to 5.70–6.95% and any-local rejection to 6.25–7.85%. These dependent-site results measure sensitivity to a violated independence assumption. The minimum attainable p-value with 39 simulations is 0.025. The archive includes counts and uncertainty intervals at thresholds of 1%, 5% and 10%.

**Maltese application.** We reconstructed the landscape hypotheses of Silva & Lomsdalen (2025) using the packaged observations for all 32 structures. All 64 entrance endpoints agreed with supplementary Table S1. We used normal measurement densities centred on the frame midpoints, with standard deviations equal to one quarter of the opening width. The terrain-aspect reconstruction uses the available 5 m Malta DTM, an eight-neighbour slope calculation and cell aspects within 30 m of each entrance. The wind reconstruction digitises the 12 frequency sectors in Galdies (2011), distributes each sector's mass uniformly within its bounds and rotates directions by 180°. The winter sunlight reconstruction samples apparent solar-centre azimuths at one-minute intervals between the autumn and spring equinoxes of 3000 BCE at the mean temple location. Each model used a 0.5° candidate grid.

| Reconstructed hypothesis | Global p-value, 9,999 simulations |
|:---|---:|
| Site-specific terrain aspect | 0.0259 |
| Protection from the wind | 0.0007 |
| Exposure to winter sunlight | 0.0001 |

These values belong to the reconstructed inputs and current scoring convention. The original simulation draws and exact historical model tables were unavailable in the retrieved supplement. The raster operator, wind digitisation, solar viewpoint and discretisation can affect the comparison. The archive contains the inputs, local intervals, and a 499-simulation public-interface replay verifying the longer run. [Published study and supplement](https://doi.org/10.1007/s12520-025-02208-4). [Source wind rose, Figure 19](https://nso.gov.mt/wp-content/uploads/The_Climate_of_Malta.pdf).

[Download S02 scripts and results](archives/S02-9008.zip).

## H07 · Coverage of partial photographic skylines {#h07-panorama-coverage}

A photograph covering 330° through north to 30° supplies no terrain height at 180°. In the archived manual example, 2.0.9007 returned a finite declination distribution spanning −39.302° to −35.032° for a uniform bearing of 180° ± 1°, and a sunrise at 92.481° on 20 March 2026. Direct altitude lookup already returned a missing value at 180°. The shifted profile rows intended to support interpolation at north also allowed other consumers to interpolate across the missing sector.

Build 2.0.9008 checks coverage at the point of use. In the archived example both the unsupported transformation and the sunrise search now give explicit coverage errors. The complete test suite also supplied an independent level mask with known edges.

| Operation | Verified behaviour |
|:---|:---|
| `hor2alt()` | Both edges and bearings inside the photographed arc return finite values. Outside bearings return missing values. |
| `coordtrans()` | Inside and north-wrapping densities agree with the complete level skyline. Positive density crossing an edge, or lying wholly outside, raises an error. Zero SPD tails outside coverage were accepted in the tested case. |
| `riseset()`, `star.phases()`, `spatial.equinox()` | Full-sky searches reject a partial photograph. The corresponding full-profile controls run successfully. |
| `exportHor()` | Partial photographs are rejected for both textured and numerical landscape export. Both modes accept the full photograph. |

All 33 assertions and the archived replay passed. The results concern the recorded azimuth sector of an imported panorama. They do not calibrate the photograph's angular accuracy. [Download H07 fixtures, scripts and results](archives/H07-9008.zip).

## W01 · Geometry and labels in graphical outputs {#w01-plot-geometry}

The study recorded the coordinates and labels passed to R's graphics routines while rendering the figures on real PNG devices. Independent fixtures specified the bearings, spherical bounds of rising and setting sectors, known skylines, disjoint density intervals, local probabilities and season boundaries. Numeric comparisons used an absolute tolerance of 0.0000001 in plotting coordinates.

| Output | Quantities checked |
|:---|:---|
| Compass and bearing intervals | True-bearing spokes, cardinal labels, both edges of a dated celestial sector, same-target labels across epochs, and an opening spanning north |
| Horizons | Flat and raised skyline ordinates, clipped azimuth range, and the foreground under natural, colour and monochrome sky overlays |
| PDFs and SPDs | Separate shaded regions at the stored highest-density limits and exact summed-density curve coordinates |
| Significance results | The envelope, global p-value, excess and deficit endpoints, and a single wrapped interval drawn in two segments on a full turn. Printing retains one interval and its adjusted probability. |
| Stellar phases | Ring and strip season boundaries, individual transition leaders, quarterly landmarks and correct star, site and epoch labels |

All 192 geometry and label assertions passed, along with direct checks of the printed output. The suite generated 50 renders. The main fixtures used 96 and 180 dpi, with additional label checks at 120 dpi. This is a numerical presentation check on specified fixtures, not a guarantee against label collisions with arbitrary inputs or device sizes. [Download W01 scripts, results and representative renders](archives/W01-9008.zip).

All three studies used the [2.0.9008 source archive](archives/skyscapeR_2.0.9008.tar.gz), SHA-256 `de09a5ba2f6eb6ee4e702776dacd9ad0d6b4cd3bda9cdcd43825f9fc629d3902`.

## A05 · Solar dates and limiting declinations {#a05-solar-limits}

A05 distinguishes the civil day on which the Sun reaches a declination, the instant of a named season, and the direction of a crossing at a particular site. We tested each quantity against its own reference. All 121 assertions passed on 2.0.9009.

| Quantity | Reference and result |
|:---|:---|
| Solar civil dates | A six-hour [JPL Horizons](https://ssd.jpl.nasa.gov/horizons/) geocentric apparent-of-date table supplied 12 crossings at six declinations in 2000. [`solar.date()`](help/solar.date.html) matched every UT civil day. As a separate diagnostic, solving against the package's underlying solar ephemeris gave differences of at most 2.65 seconds from the interpolated JPL roots. The largest occurred close to the June turning point. |
| Calendar branches | Independent bracketing on a quarter-day grid checked 2000 CE and 3250 BCE in Gregorian and Julian calendars. At the maximum declination a tangency gave one passage, an immediately lower target gave two, and an unreachable target gave none. A civil-year boundary fixture gave three passages. |
| Named seasons | The four named season dates matched the [US Naval Observatory 2000 record](https://aa.usno.navy.mil/data/Earth_Seasons). Underlying apparent-longitude roots differed by at most 26 seconds from the minute-rounded reference. The public labels report civil days. |
| Northern and southern terrain limits | The direct spherical reference searched a dense grid throughout each specified sector. An interior crest gave a maximum of 48.5884° and an interior trough gave a minimum of −47.7023°. Both functions agreed within 0.00028°. The tests also covered level terrain at four latitudes. |
| Spatial equinox | An independent hour-angle track and sign-bracketed roots checked northern and southern sites, a flat horizon and separate east and west ridges. Rising and setting midpoints and derived declinations agreed within 0.000003°. The high-latitude case correctly lacked the pair of crossings needed for a midpoint. These checks disabled refraction and parallax to isolate geometry. |
| Zenith and anti-zenith | At geometric overhead and underfoot the parallax correction vanishes. Build 2.0.9009 uses the obliquity of the supplied year for tropical eligibility. The fixtures include both tropical boundaries, modern and prehistoric epochs, and an unreachable polar site. |

The prehistoric date checks use an independent root search with the same Swiss ephemeris. The JPL and USNO comparisons apply to the modern cases tested. [Download the A05 scripts, reference data and results](archives/A05-9009.zip).

## A08 · Target screening and dated bands {#a08-target-ranges}

A measured band can intersect a target briefly, more than once, or exactly at a turning point. We compared [`findTargets()`](help/findTargets.html) with independent annual stellar samples and a separate line-segment intersection calculation. For solar and lunar limits, the reference evaluates January obliquity and the local parallax term for every integer year. All 129 assertions passed on 2.0.9009.

**Stellar membership.** In a 30–42 CE search, a narrow band around a turning point for Sirius returned *35–35 CE* and *38–39 CE* after rounding the interpolated boundaries to years. The exact annual maximum gave one contact in 36 CE. The study also tested magnitude inclusion and exclusion, one-year searches, catalogue identifiers and aliases, and the pairing of colours and styles with their targets. The implementation treats stellar differences within 0.0000001° of an edge as a contact. The reference shares the stellar ephemeris. This study validates selection and aggregation; stellar positions at subannual extrema remain outside this model.

**Solar and lunar bounds.** Earlier builds could collapse a short overlay range to one sampled value and lose the observing site's parallax when calculating a dated envelope. At 50° N over astronomical years −3400 to −3100 the old southern major lunar overlay gave approximately −29.34° to −29.32°. The annual local limits were −30.08° to −30.05°. The largest endpoint error in the fixtures was 0.7334°. Build 2.0.9009 reproduced the annual local bounds, including both endpoints, for one-year, short, modern and prehistoric ranges. Spherical inversion of the returned orbit coordinates recovered their input declinations.

Candidate selection now uses unrounded declinations. The two-decimal limits are display values. Solar zenith/anti-zenith screening uses the archaeological period and requires a reachable passage. The spatial-equinox candidate uses the rising and setting solutions from the endpoint epochs; this particular candidate does not claim to enclose every intermediate year's terrain midpoint. [Download the A08 scripts and results](archives/A08-9009.zip).

## W02 · End-to-end field-to-sky replay {#w02-field-to-sky}

W02 replayed the Malta workflows on the archived 2.0.9004 build and on the final build, with intermediate tables for field reduction, sightlines, transformed densities, inference, screening, seasonal dates, crossings and reconstructed sky position. The Maltese entrances are published **true bearings**. The raw compass and solar-circle observations in this study are separately constructed controls. They do not reconstruct the original instrument notebooks.

| Handoff | Result |
|:---|:---|
| Raw field controls | A target circle of 2.25° and solar circle of 358.75° give 161.23° at the Malta control site. The archived matrix call returned −558.77°, equivalent modulo 360°, and its single-vector call failed. In a two-site fixture the old matrix reshaping also changed the actual assigned coordinates. The corrected paired bearings were 161.23° and 141.72°, each matching the independent circle-difference calculation. |
| Mnajdra South | The edges 90.94° and 99.14° sampled skyline heights of 4.40° and 3.45°. The corresponding declinations were +1.71° and −5.48° on both builds. The first divergence along the published-bearing route was in the azimuth PDFs. The final 68% declination HDR comprised −4.75° to −1.95° and −0.90° to +1.00°. |
| Group inference | The replay preserved entrance/profile order for all 17 Ġgantija-phase entrances. The 39-simulation controls exercised both significance routes with fixed inputs and seeds. Separately, the full vignette replay used 500 random-orientation simulations and recovered the bundled global p = 2/501, the excess at −33.7° to −28.6° (adjusted p = 2/501), and the excess at −49.4° to −48.2° (adjusted p = 279/501). |
| Skorba West | Gacrux was returned by the screen for the archived significant band. The modeled heliacal rising date was 12 October 3250 BCE, Julian calendar. On the fifth subsequent morning the terrain crossing was at 03:33:11 UT and azimuth 129.9315°. Twenty minutes later the sketch placed Gacrux at azimuth 132.9940°, altitude 4.2488°, between the entrance edges 128.55° and 138.07° and 2.41° above the recorded skyline. A separate spherical transform at the saved instant reproduced the sketch coordinates. |

**Sensitivity.** Swapping the Mnajdra South and Skorba West profiles changed only the corresponding two mean declinations, by 2.219° and 1.448°. The numeric calculation followed the supplied order, so correct site pairing remains the analyst's responsibility. Rebuilding the PDFs with refraction off shifted their means by 0.146° on average. The seeded random test on the original stored PDFs retained its original results when the session setting changed. A north-crossing density integrated to one. An out-of-sector photographic transformation returned a finite curve on the archived build and an explicit coverage error on the final build.

All 26 workflow assertions passed, alongside the site-row and terminal-position controls. Agreement across this workflow establishes numerical continuity of its inputs and outputs. It provides neither a measurement of ancient naked-eye visibility nor evidence of intentional alignment. [Download W02 scripts, per-stage tables and version comparisons](archives/W02-9009.zip).

These three studies use the [installable 2.0.9009 source](archives/skyscapeR_2.0.9009.tar.gz), SHA-256 `1c5b347aabb1c8d3bdd3bc27d1d9d11c1cb12b550424df4dc22d6bcaff91b0a9`.
